passages.title: David laments Saul and Jonathan
passages.summary: David is back in Ziklag when a man arrives from Saul’s camp. The man is an Amalekite, and he carries Saul’s crown and bracelet. He says the wounded Saul asked him for a final blow. David and his men tear their clothes and fast until evening. David has the man put to death for killing the LORD’s anointed. Then David sings a lament for Saul and Jonathan. Three times it cries, “How the mighty have fallen!” He orders the people of Judah to learn it.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older Church manual says the messenger lied about killing Saul. On what evidence does David sentence him in verse 16?

contextNote.title: The messenger's account cannot purchase royal favor
contextNote.text: First Samuel 31:4 says Saul fell on his own sword. The Amalekite tells a different story and brings the crown as proof. David later says the man expected a reward (4:10). In verse 16 David judges him by his own mouth. The news removes David’s enemy and opens the throne. David still answers it with mourning and a song. The lament praises Saul and never mentions the years of pursuit.

passages.title: Two kingdoms and the battle at Gibeon
passages.summary: David asks the LORD and moves to Hebron. The men of Judah anoint him king there. He thanks Jabesh Gilead for burying Saul. Abner, Saul’s general, makes Saul’s son Ishbosheth king over the other tribes. The two armies meet at the pool of Gibeon. A contest of twelve against twelve turns into a battle. Joab’s brother Asahel chases Abner, ignores two warnings, and is killed. At sunset Abner calls for a halt, and Joab stops the pursuit.

lds.text: Why does Abner ask Joab to stop the fighting?

contextNote.title: Personal pursuit helps extend a divided kingship's war
contextNote.text: Abner’s plea in verse 26 calls both armies “brothers.” He asks whether the sword must devour forever. Yet Abner proposed the deadly contest that began the day (verse 14). Joab accepts the halt and blows the trumpet (verse 28). The count is unequal: twenty dead against three hundred sixty (verses 30–31). Asahel’s death is not settled by the truce. Joab repays it in 3:27.

passages.title: Abner changes allegiance and Joab kills him
passages.summary: The war between Saul’s house and David’s house lasts a long time. Ishbosheth accuses Abner over one of Saul’s concubines. Abner is furious and offers to bring all Israel to David. David first demands Michal back, and her husband follows her weeping. Abner meets David and leaves in peace. Joab calls him back and stabs him at the gate for Asahel’s death. David curses Joab’s house and leads the mourning for Abner. He says Zeruiah’s sons are too hard for him.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: What happens to Michal and her husband when David demands her return?

contextNote.title: Public mourning separates kingship from a commander's revenge
contextNote.text: Abner’s death helps David, and people could suspect him. Verse 28 is his public denial before the LORD. He adds a curse on Joab’s house in verse 29. He walks behind the body, weeps, and fasts (verses 31–35). Verse 37 says all the people understood it was not his doing. Still he does not punish Joab. In verse 39 he admits he is too weak to control him.

passages.title: Ishbosheth is murdered
passages.summary: Ishbosheth loses courage when he hears Abner is dead. Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth is mentioned; he was lamed as a child in the flight. Two of Ishbosheth’s captains, Rechab and Baanah, enter his house at noon. They kill him on his bed and cut off his head. They carry it all night to David at Hebron. They say the LORD has avenged David on Saul’s family. David recalls the messenger he executed at Ziklag. He has the two men killed and buries the head in Abner’s tomb.

lds.text: Why does David punish men who expect a reward for killing his rival?

contextNote.title: Another murder tests the route to royal security
contextNote.text: This is the third death that clears David’s path. Saul, Abner, and now Ishbosheth are gone. Each time someone expects David to be pleased. The killers even use the LORD’s name for their act (verse 8). David answers that the LORD has already rescued him from trouble (verse 9). In verse 11 he calls his rival “a righteous person.” He will not take a throne handed to him by murder.

passages.title: David becomes king of Israel and takes Jerusalem
passages.summary: All the tribes come to Hebron and anoint David king over Israel. He is thirty years old and reigns forty years in all. He captures the stronghold of Zion from the Jebusites. Jerusalem becomes the City of David. Hiram king of Tyre sends cedar and craftsmen to build him a house. David takes more wives and has more children. The Philistines attack twice in the Valley of Rephaim. Each time David asks the LORD and wins.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies seeking divine guidance. For whose sake does verse 12 say the kingdom was raised up?

contextNote.title: A palace receives a stated public purpose
contextNote.text: Verse 12 gives the purpose of David’s success. The LORD raised his kingdom “for his people Israel’s sake.” The palace and the throne are means to that end. The next verse reports more wives and concubines (verse 13). Deuteronomy 17:17 warned kings against exactly that. The text sets the two verses together without comment. In verses 19 and 23 David asks before each battle and gets different orders.

passages.title: The ark reaches Jerusalem
passages.summary: David gathers thirty thousand men to bring the ark to Jerusalem. They carry it on a new cart, and Uzzah touches it and dies. David is angry and afraid and leaves it at Obed-Edom’s house. The LORD blesses that house for three months. David then brings the ark up with sacrifices, dancing in a linen ephod. Saul’s daughter Michal watches from a window and despises him. He blesses the people and gives everyone food. Michal mocks his display, and she has no child to her death.

lds.text: The older manual connects the ark’s handling with sacred responsibility. Its proposed motives are interpretations. What does Michal object to in verse 20?

contextNote.title: Public worship crosses expectations about royal display
contextNote.text: The chapter calls Michal “the daughter of Saul” three times (verses 16, 20, 23). It does not call her David’s wife here. In verse 20 she speaks for a king’s dignity before servants. David answers that the LORD chose him above her father (verse 21). Their history is long and painful. She loved him and saved him, then was given away and taken back. Verse 23 means no child will join the two royal houses.

passages.title: Nathan announces a promised house
passages.summary: David lives in a cedar house and wants to build one for the ark. The prophet Nathan first tells him to go ahead. That night the LORD sends Nathan back with a different word. The LORD never asked for a house of cedar. He took David from the pasture and will make David a house. A son will build the temple, and his throne will last forever. If he sins he will be disciplined, but not rejected like Saul. David sits before the LORD and asks, “Who am I?”

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects the promised house with Jesus Christ. Who will build a house for whom in verses 11–13?

contextNote.title: A promise raises the stakes of royal conduct
contextNote.text: The chapter turns on two meanings of “house.” David offers the LORD a building (verse 2). The LORD offers David a family of kings (verse 11). Verse 13 joins both: the son builds, and God secures his throne. Verses 14–15 add a limit and a guarantee. A sinning king will be punished, yet the kindness will not be removed. Even Nathan’s first answer is corrected the same night (verses 3–5).

passages.title: Wars, tribute, and royal officials
passages.summary: David defeats the Philistines and takes their chief city. He defeats Moab and puts two thirds of the captives to death. He defeats Hadadezer of Zobah and the Syrians of Damascus. He places troops in Syria and Edom, and those peoples serve him. King Toi of Hamath sends gifts of silver, gold, and bronze. David dedicates the metal to the LORD. The LORD gives him victory wherever he goes. The chapter ends with a list of his chief officers.

lds.text: How does David’s growing rule affect the people his armies defeat?

contextNote.title: A claim about justice stands beside conquest
contextNote.text: Verse 15 says David did justice and right “for all his people.” The claim concerns Israel. The verses before it describe the defeated very differently. Moab’s captives are measured for death, and the rest pay tribute (verse 2). Syria and Edom become subject peoples (verses 6 and 14). The text credits the victories to the LORD and does not judge the methods. Verses 16–18 show a kingdom with fixed offices for the first time.

passages.title: Mephibosheth receives land and a place at the table
passages.summary: David asks whether anyone is left from Saul’s house. He wants to show kindness for Jonathan’s sake. Ziba, a servant of Saul’s house, names Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth, who is lame. David sends for him from Lo Debar. Mephibosheth falls on his face before the king. David tells him not to fear and restores all Saul’s land to him. Ziba and his household will farm it. Mephibosheth will eat at the king’s table like one of his sons.

lds.text: The older manual studies David’s kindness to Jonathan’s son. What does Mephibosheth call himself in verse 8?

contextNote.title: A royal promise changes the meaning of vulnerability
contextNote.text: New kings in these books often wiped out the old king’s family. First Kings 15:29 and 16:11 give examples. Mephibosheth has reason to fear, and David tells him not to (verse 7). His words in verse 8 are those of a man expecting nothing. David acts on his oath to Jonathan in 1 Samuel 20:14–15. He gives land for income and a seat for honor. The chapter opens and closes by noting that the man is lame.

passages.title: Humiliated envoys and war with Ammon
passages.summary: The king of Ammon dies, and David sends men to comfort his son Hanun. Hanun’s princes say the visitors are spies. Hanun shaves half of each man’s beard and cuts their clothes at the hips. David lets the shamed men wait at Jericho until their beards grow. Ammon hires Syrian armies. Joab splits his forces with his brother Abishai, and the Syrians flee. Hadadezer brings more Syrians from beyond the River. David defeats them, and they make peace with Israel.

lds.text: How could Hanun have tested his advisers’ claim before acting?

contextNote.title: Suspected motives turn an act of condolence into war
contextNote.text: The princes in verse 3 offer a suspicion and no evidence. Hanun acts on it at once. His treatment of the envoys is a public insult to their king. David shields the men from further shame (verse 5). Ammon sees it has made itself hated (verse 6). It hires soldiers instead of making amends. By verse 18 one untested suspicion has cost many thousands of lives.

passages.title: David takes Bathsheba and arranges Uriah’s death
passages.summary: In spring David sends Joab to besiege Rabbah and stays in Jerusalem. From his roof he sees a woman bathing. She is Bathsheba, wife of Uriah the Hittite, one of his soldiers. David sends for her, lies with her, and she becomes pregnant. He calls Uriah home, but Uriah will not go to his house during war. David sends him back with a letter to Joab ordering his death. Uriah is killed at the city wall with other men. David marries Bathsheba, and the thing displeases the LORD.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks readers to examine David's choices and responsibility. Who carries the letter of verse 15 to Joab (verse 14)?

contextNote.title: A written command transfers violence through officials
contextNote.text: The chapter is full of the word “sent.” David sends for news, for the woman, for Uriah, and for his death. Uriah carries his own death order in his hand (verse 14). Verse 15 makes Joab and the army the tools of a private crime. Other soldiers die with Uriah (verse 17). Uriah, a foreigner, keeps the soldier’s discipline that the king has dropped (verse 11). The only judgment comes in the last line of verse 27.

passages.title: Nathan confronts David and the child dies
passages.summary: The LORD sends Nathan to David with a story. A rich man took a poor man’s only lamb to feed a guest. David says the man deserves to die. Nathan answers, “You are the man!” The sword will never leave David’s house, and his own wives will be taken. David confesses, and Nathan says he will not die, but the child will. David fasts for seven days until the child dies. Later Bathsheba bears Solomon, and David captures Rabbah.

lds.text: The older manual compares verse 13 with the Joseph Smith Translation. That version changes Nathan’s words about David’s sin. What does David say about the rich man before verse 7?

contextNote.title: A story makes unequal power visible
contextNote.text: Nathan lets David judge the case before he knows it is his own. The poor man’s lamb was “like a daughter” to him (verse 3). David’s anger at the rich man is real (verses 5–6). Verse 7 turns his verdict back on him. The LORD’s speech lists what he gave David (verses 7–8). Verse 9 then says what David took. The penalties in verses 10–11 match the crimes: the sword and the wives.

passages.title: Amnon assaults Tamar and Absalom takes revenge
passages.summary: David’s son Amnon desires his half sister Tamar. On a cousin’s advice he pretends to be ill and asks her to bring food. He seizes her, and she pleads with him. He rapes her, then hates her and has her thrown out. Tamar tears her royal robe and goes away crying. Her brother Absalom takes her into his house. David is very angry but does nothing. Two years later Absalom has Amnon killed and flees to Geshur.

lds.text: What does Tamar ask Amnon to do? Who fails to protect her?

contextNote.title: Tamar's speech must shape the reading of this assault
contextNote.text: Tamar’s speech in verses 12–13 is clear and reasoned. She names the act as a disgrace in Israel. She names her own shame and his ruin. She even offers a lawful way through the king. Verse 14 says he would not listen. Her father is angry and silent (verse 21). Her brother tells her to keep quiet (verse 20).

passages.title: The woman of Tekoa and Absalom’s return
passages.summary: Joab sees that David longs for Absalom. He sends a wise woman from Tekoa to the king in mourning clothes. She says one of her sons killed the other in a fight. Her clan now demands the life of the son who is left. David promises to protect him. She then asks why the king does not bring back his own banished son. David guesses that Joab is behind it and lets Absalom return. For two years Absalom may not see the king’s face.

lds.text: How does Joab use the woman’s story to change David’s decision?

contextNote.title: A constructed legal case directs a family decision
contextNote.text: The woman’s method copies Nathan’s in chapter 12. She wins a ruling on an invented case and then applies it. Verse 14 is her main argument. Death is final, like water spilled on the ground. God, she says, finds ways to bring the banished back. Her case differs from Absalom’s, who planned his killing for two years (13:23–28). David brings him back but will not see him (verse 24).

passages.title: Absalom gathers support and David leaves Jerusalem
passages.summary: Absalom gets a chariot, horses, and fifty runners. He stands by the gate and meets people who bring cases to the king. He tells each one that his claim is good and no one will hear it. So he steals the hearts of Israel. After four years he goes to Hebron and has himself declared king. David flees Jerusalem with his household and loyal foreign troops. He sends the ark back to the city with the priests. He climbs the Mount of Olives weeping and sends Hushai to act as a spy.

lds.text: How does Absalom use promises of justice to win support?

contextNote.title: A claim to fair judgment becomes a route to power
contextNote.text: Absalom never hears a case in this chapter. He tells every visitor the same thing: your claim is right (verse 3). In verse 4 he wishes aloud to be judge. He greets people as equals and will not let them bow (verse 5). The text does not say whether the courts were truly neglected. Verse 6 calls the result theft. David, by contrast, refuses to use the ark for his own cause (verses 25–26).

passages.title: Ziba’s accusation, Shimei’s curses, and Absalom’s public act
passages.summary: Ziba meets the fleeing king with donkeys, bread, fruit, and wine. He says Mephibosheth stayed in Jerusalem hoping to gain Saul’s kingdom. David gives Ziba all of Mephibosheth’s property. At Bahurim a man of Saul’s family named Shimei curses David and throws stones. Abishai wants to cut off his head. David says to leave him; perhaps the LORD told him to curse. Absalom enters Jerusalem, and Hushai pretends to serve him. On Ahithophel’s advice Absalom takes his father’s concubines in public.

lds.text: Whose account does David hear before giving Ziba the land?

contextNote.title: A hurried property decision rests on an unheard accusation
contextNote.text: David decides a property case in verse 4 on one man’s word. The accused is absent and cannot answer. Ziba arrives with gifts, and he gains from the charge he brings. Mephibosheth’s side is heard only in 19:24–27. David lost support to a son who promised fair hearings (15:4). Here he gives an unfair one himself. With Shimei in verses 10–12 he is far more patient.

passages.title: Hushai’s counsel and the messengers’ escape
passages.summary: Ahithophel advises Absalom to strike David that night with twelve thousand men. Hushai argues for waiting and gathering all Israel. Absalom prefers Hushai’s advice, as the LORD intended. Hushai sends warning to David through the priests’ two sons. A boy sees them, and they hide in a well at Bahurim. A woman covers the well and sends the searchers away. David crosses the Jordan that night, and Ahithophel hangs himself. At Mahanaim three men bring beds, bowls, and food to David’s people.

lds.text: Which people bring food and other help to David’s group?

contextNote.title: Ordinary households help carry politically dangerous knowledge
contextNote.text: David’s survival depends on a chain of ordinary people. Hushai tells the priests, and a servant girl carries the word (verses 15–17). In verse 18 a householder’s well becomes the hiding place. His wife covers it and misleads the searchers (verses 19–20). Bahurim is also Shimei’s town (16:5), so one village holds both sides. Verse 14 gives the writer’s view of the cause. Machir, who brings supplies in verse 27, once sheltered Mephibosheth (9:4).

passages.title: Absalom dies and David grieves
passages.summary: David divides his army under Joab, Abishai, and Ittai. The men will not let him fight. He orders the three to deal gently with Absalom, and all the soldiers hear it. David’s men win in the forest of Ephraim. Absalom’s head catches in an oak, and his mule runs on. A soldier refuses to touch him, but Joab stabs him. Two runners carry the news to the king. David asks only about Absalom and weeps, “My son, my son!”

lds.text: Why does David’s grief differ from his soldiers’ joy over victory?

contextNote.title: The king's family wish conflicts with his army's goal
contextNote.text: Verse 5 notes that the whole army heard the king’s order. A soldier quotes it to Joab in verse 12 as his reason for holding back. Joab knows the order and breaks it (verse 14). He acts for the kingdom: a living Absalom is a living revolt. David asks both runners the same question (verses 29 and 32). His question is a father’s, not a king’s. Verse 33 gives his answer to the victory.

passages.title: David returns and hears competing claims
passages.summary: Joab tells David that his weeping shames the men who saved him. David sits in the gate, and the people come to him. He invites Judah to bring him back and promises Joab’s post to Amasa. Shimei begs forgiveness at the Jordan, and David spares him. Mephibosheth comes unwashed and says Ziba deceived him. David tells the two to divide the land. Old Barzillai declines a place at court and sends Chimham. Israel and Judah then quarrel over who has more claim to the king.

lds.text: Which disputes remain after David returns to rule?

contextNote.title: Restored rule does not settle every disputed claim
contextNote.text: Two men have told David opposite stories about the same land. Verse 24 supports Mephibosheth: he had not groomed himself since the king left. In verse 29 David cuts the question short. He splits the land and decides nothing about the truth. Mephibosheth answers that Ziba may take it all (verse 30). The pardon of Shimei is also not final (1 Kings 2:8–9). The quarrel in verses 41–43 leads straight into the next revolt.

passages.title: Sheba’s revolt and the wise woman of Abel
passages.summary: Sheba, a man of Benjamin, calls Israel to leave David, and the northern tribes follow. David sets apart the ten concubines Absalom took. Amasa is slow to gather Judah’s army. Joab greets Amasa as a brother and stabs him. Joab’s army besieges Sheba in the town of Abel. A wise woman calls to Joab from the wall. She persuades the town to throw Sheba’s head over to him. Joab withdraws, and a list of David’s officers follows.

lds.text: The older manual states that David’s concubines were not responsible for Absalom’s violation. What does the woman accuse Joab of in verse 19?

contextNote.title: A city's voice challenges a commander's method
contextNote.text: Joab is battering the wall when a woman asks to speak (verses 15–16). In verse 19 she names her town “a mother in Israel.” She calls it part of the LORD’s inheritance. Joab must then state what he really wants: one man (verse 21). She takes that to the people “in her wisdom” (verse 22). One death ends a siege that would have killed many. Abigail and the woman of Tekoa also stopped armed men with words.

passages.title: Rizpah guards the dead and warriors defend David
passages.summary: A famine lasts three years, and David asks the LORD why. The answer is that Saul killed Gibeonites, breaking Israel’s old oath. The Gibeonites ask for seven of Saul’s male descendants. David spares Mephibosheth and hands over seven others. They are hanged on a hill at the start of barley harvest. Rizpah, mother of two of them, guards the bodies until the rain comes. David hears of it and buries the bones with Saul’s and Jonathan’s. Four giants later fall to David’s men.

lds.text: The older manual questions the executions under the law against punishing children for parents’ sins. What does Rizpah do in verse 10?

contextNote.title: A mother's vigil changes the public handling of death
contextNote.text: Rizpah could not stop the executions. Verse 10 shows what she could do. She stays on the rock from harvest until rain, day and night. Deuteronomy 21:22–23 required burial the same day. Her watch is reported to the king (verse 11). Only then does David gather the bones and bury them properly (verses 12–14). Verse 14 places God’s answer for the land after that burial.

passages.title: David’s song of deliverance
passages.summary: David sings this song after the LORD rescues him from Saul and all his enemies. He calls the LORD his rock, fortress, and shield. Death’s waves surrounded him, and he cried out. The earth shook, and the LORD came down in storm and fire. He drew David out of deep waters. David says the LORD rewarded his clean hands. With God’s help he can run through a troop and leap a wall. The song ends with kindness to David and his descendants forever.

lds.text: How does David’s song compare with his choices elsewhere in the book?

contextNote.title: A royal song interprets strength as received help
contextNote.text: The song is nearly the same as Psalm 18. Verse 36 credits David’s strength to gifts: a shield and God’s gentleness. He says that gentleness, not his own skill, made him great. The heading in verse 1 ties the song to his rescue from Saul. Verses 21–25 claim clean hands and kept ways. That fits the David of the cave, not of chapter 11. The book places the song here and leaves the contrast for the reader.

passages.title: Last words and remembered warriors
passages.summary: David’s last words say a ruler must be just and fear God. Such a ruler is like morning light after rain. God has made a lasting covenant with his house. The chapter then lists David’s mighty men and their deeds. One stood alone in a field and fought until his hand stuck to his sword. Three broke through Philistine lines to bring David water from Bethlehem’s well. Benaiah killed a lion in a pit on a snowy day. The list of the Thirty ends with Uriah the Hittite.

lds.text: How do the warriors’ actions show the risks of serving a king?

contextNote.title: Refusing a gift can recognize another person's risk
contextNote.text: David’s wish in verse 15 is spoken aloud, not given as an order. Three men risk their lives to grant it (verse 16). In verse 17 he will not drink. He calls the water the blood of the men who went. He pours it out to the LORD, as blood was poured out. The act honors their risk more than drinking would. The list ends in verse 39 with the name of a man David betrayed.

passages.title: The census, plague, and Araunah’s threshing floor
passages.summary: The LORD is angry with Israel, and David is moved to count the people. Joab objects, but the king insists. The count takes almost ten months. Then David’s heart troubles him, and he confesses. The prophet Gad offers three punishments, and David chooses to fall into the LORD’s hand. A plague kills seventy thousand. The angel stops at the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. David buys the floor, builds an altar, and the plague ends.

lds.text: The older Church manual compares this account with First Chronicles 21. Why does David refuse Araunah’s gift in verse 24?

contextNote.title: An offering must cost the giver something
contextNote.text: Araunah offers the floor, the oxen, and the wood for free (verses 22–23). David’s refusal in verse 24 gives a rule for offerings. A gift to God that costs the giver nothing is no gift. The plague came through David’s own act (verse 10). A free altar would move the cost onto another man. In verse 17 David asks that the punishment fall on him and his house. Second Chronicles 3:1 places the later temple at this floor.

events.title: David laments Saul and Jonathan
events.summary: David is back in Ziklag when a man arrives from Saul’s camp. The man is an Amalekite, and he carries Saul’s crown and bracelet. He says the wounded Saul asked him for a final blow. David and his men tear their clothes and fast until evening. David has the man put to death for killing the LORD’s anointed. Then David sings a lament for Saul and Jonathan. Three times it cries, “How the mighty have fallen!” He orders the people of Judah to learn it.
events.detail: First Samuel 31:4 says Saul fell on his own sword. The Amalekite tells a different story and brings the crown as proof. David later says the man expected a reward (4:10). In verse 16 David judges him by his own mouth. The news removes David’s enemy and opens the throne. David still answers it with mourning and a song. The lament praises Saul and never mentions the years of pursuit.

events.title: Two kingdoms and the battle at Gibeon
events.summary: David asks the LORD and moves to Hebron. The men of Judah anoint him king there. He thanks Jabesh Gilead for burying Saul. Abner, Saul’s general, makes Saul’s son Ishbosheth king over the other tribes. The two armies meet at the pool of Gibeon. A contest of twelve against twelve turns into a battle. Joab’s brother Asahel chases Abner, ignores two warnings, and is killed. At sunset Abner calls for a halt, and Joab stops the pursuit.
events.detail: Abner’s plea in verse 26 calls both armies “brothers.” He asks whether the sword must devour forever. Yet Abner proposed the deadly contest that began the day (verse 14). Joab accepts the halt and blows the trumpet (verse 28). The count is unequal: twenty dead against three hundred sixty (verses 30–31). Asahel’s death is not settled by the truce. Joab repays it in 3:27.

lds.text: Why does Abner ask Joab to stop the fighting?

events.title: Abner changes allegiance and Joab kills him
events.summary: The war between Saul’s house and David’s house lasts a long time. Ishbosheth accuses Abner over one of Saul’s concubines. Abner is furious and offers to bring all Israel to David. David first demands Michal back, and her husband follows her weeping. Abner meets David and leaves in peace. Joab calls him back and stabs him at the gate for Asahel’s death. David curses Joab’s house and leads the mourning for Abner. He says Zeruiah’s sons are too hard for him.
events.detail: Abner’s death helps David, and people could suspect him. Verse 28 is his public denial before the LORD. He adds a curse on Joab’s house in verse 29. He walks behind the body, weeps, and fasts (verses 31–35). Verse 37 says all the people understood it was not his doing. Still he does not punish Joab. In verse 39 he admits he is too weak to control him.

events.title: Ishbosheth is murdered
events.summary: Ishbosheth loses courage when he hears Abner is dead. Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth is mentioned; he was lamed as a child in the flight. Two of Ishbosheth’s captains, Rechab and Baanah, enter his house at noon. They kill him on his bed and cut off his head. They carry it all night to David at Hebron. They say the LORD has avenged David on Saul’s family. David recalls the messenger he executed at Ziklag. He has the two men killed and buries the head in Abner’s tomb.
events.detail: This is the third death that clears David’s path. Saul, Abner, and now Ishbosheth are gone. Each time someone expects David to be pleased. The killers even use the LORD’s name for their act (verse 8). David answers that the LORD has already rescued him from trouble (verse 9). In verse 11 he calls his rival “a righteous person.” He will not take a throne handed to him by murder.

events.title: David becomes king of Israel and takes Jerusalem
events.summary: All the tribes come to Hebron and anoint David king over Israel. He is thirty years old and reigns forty years in all. He captures the stronghold of Zion from the Jebusites. Jerusalem becomes the City of David. Hiram king of Tyre sends cedar and craftsmen to build him a house. David takes more wives and has more children. The Philistines attack twice in the Valley of Rephaim. Each time David asks the LORD and wins.
events.detail: Verse 12 gives the purpose of David’s success. The LORD raised his kingdom “for his people Israel’s sake.” The palace and the throne are means to that end. The next verse reports more wives and concubines (verse 13). Deuteronomy 17:17 warned kings against exactly that. The text sets the two verses together without comment. In verses 19 and 23 David asks before each battle and gets different orders.

events.title: The ark reaches Jerusalem
events.summary: David gathers thirty thousand men to bring the ark to Jerusalem. They carry it on a new cart, and Uzzah touches it and dies. David is angry and afraid and leaves it at Obed-Edom’s house. The LORD blesses that house for three months. David then brings the ark up with sacrifices, dancing in a linen ephod. Saul’s daughter Michal watches from a window and despises him. He blesses the people and gives everyone food. Michal mocks his display, and she has no child to her death.
events.detail: The chapter calls Michal “the daughter of Saul” three times (verses 16, 20, 23). It does not call her David’s wife here. In verse 20 she speaks for a king’s dignity before servants. David answers that the LORD chose him above her father (verse 21). Their history is long and painful. She loved him and saved him, then was given away and taken back. Verse 23 means no child will join the two royal houses.

events.title: Nathan announces a promised house
events.summary: David lives in a cedar house and wants to build one for the ark. The prophet Nathan first tells him to go ahead. That night the LORD sends Nathan back with a different word. The LORD never asked for a house of cedar. He took David from the pasture and will make David a house. A son will build the temple, and his throne will last forever. If he sins he will be disciplined, but not rejected like Saul. David sits before the LORD and asks, “Who am I?”
events.detail: The chapter turns on two meanings of “house.” David offers the LORD a building (verse 2). The LORD offers David a family of kings (verse 11). Verse 13 joins both: the son builds, and God secures his throne. Verses 14–15 add a limit and a guarantee. A sinning king will be punished, yet the kindness will not be removed. Even Nathan’s first answer is corrected the same night (verses 3–5).

events.title: Wars, tribute, and royal officials
events.summary: David defeats the Philistines and takes their chief city. He defeats Moab and puts two thirds of the captives to death. He defeats Hadadezer of Zobah and the Syrians of Damascus. He places troops in Syria and Edom, and those peoples serve him. King Toi of Hamath sends gifts of silver, gold, and bronze. David dedicates the metal to the LORD. The LORD gives him victory wherever he goes. The chapter ends with a list of his chief officers.
events.detail: Verse 15 says David did justice and right “for all his people.” The claim concerns Israel. The verses before it describe the defeated very differently. Moab’s captives are measured for death, and the rest pay tribute (verse 2). Syria and Edom become subject peoples (verses 6 and 14). The text credits the victories to the LORD and does not judge the methods. Verses 16–18 show a kingdom with fixed offices for the first time.

events.title: Mephibosheth receives land and a place at the table
events.summary: David asks whether anyone is left from Saul’s house. He wants to show kindness for Jonathan’s sake. Ziba, a servant of Saul’s house, names Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth, who is lame. David sends for him from Lo Debar. Mephibosheth falls on his face before the king. David tells him not to fear and restores all Saul’s land to him. Ziba and his household will farm it. Mephibosheth will eat at the king’s table like one of his sons.
events.detail: New kings in these books often wiped out the old king’s family. First Kings 15:29 and 16:11 give examples. Mephibosheth has reason to fear, and David tells him not to (verse 7). His words in verse 8 are those of a man expecting nothing. David acts on his oath to Jonathan in 1 Samuel 20:14–15. He gives land for income and a seat for honor. The chapter opens and closes by noting that the man is lame.

events.title: Humiliated envoys and war with Ammon
events.summary: The king of Ammon dies, and David sends men to comfort his son Hanun. Hanun’s princes say the visitors are spies. Hanun shaves half of each man’s beard and cuts their clothes at the hips. David lets the shamed men wait at Jericho until their beards grow. Ammon hires Syrian armies. Joab splits his forces with his brother Abishai, and the Syrians flee. Hadadezer brings more Syrians from beyond the River. David defeats them, and they make peace with Israel.
events.detail: The princes in verse 3 offer a suspicion and no evidence. Hanun acts on it at once. His treatment of the envoys is a public insult to their king. David shields the men from further shame (verse 5). Ammon sees it has made itself hated (verse 6). It hires soldiers instead of making amends. By verse 18 one untested suspicion has cost many thousands of lives.

events.title: David takes Bathsheba and arranges Uriah’s death
events.summary: In spring David sends Joab to besiege Rabbah and stays in Jerusalem. From his roof he sees a woman bathing. She is Bathsheba, wife of Uriah the Hittite, one of his soldiers. David sends for her, lies with her, and she becomes pregnant. He calls Uriah home, but Uriah will not go to his house during war. David sends him back with a letter to Joab ordering his death. Uriah is killed at the city wall with other men. David marries Bathsheba, and the thing displeases the LORD.
events.detail: The chapter is full of the word “sent.” David sends for news, for the woman, for Uriah, and for his death. Uriah carries his own death order in his hand (verse 14). Verse 15 makes Joab and the army the tools of a private crime. Other soldiers die with Uriah (verse 17). Uriah, a foreigner, keeps the soldier’s discipline that the king has dropped (verse 11). The only judgment comes in the last line of verse 27.

events.title: Nathan confronts David and the child dies
events.summary: The LORD sends Nathan to David with a story. A rich man took a poor man’s only lamb to feed a guest. David says the man deserves to die. Nathan answers, “You are the man!” The sword will never leave David’s house, and his own wives will be taken. David confesses, and Nathan says he will not die, but the child will. David fasts for seven days until the child dies. Later Bathsheba bears Solomon, and David captures Rabbah.
events.detail: Nathan lets David judge the case before he knows it is his own. The poor man’s lamb was “like a daughter” to him (verse 3). David’s anger at the rich man is real (verses 5–6). Verse 7 turns his verdict back on him. The LORD’s speech lists what he gave David (verses 7–8). Verse 9 then says what David took. The penalties in verses 10–11 match the crimes: the sword and the wives.

events.title: Amnon assaults Tamar and Absalom takes revenge
events.summary: David’s son Amnon desires his half sister Tamar. On a cousin’s advice he pretends to be ill and asks her to bring food. He seizes her, and she pleads with him. He rapes her, then hates her and has her thrown out. Tamar tears her royal robe and goes away crying. Her brother Absalom takes her into his house. David is very angry but does nothing. Two years later Absalom has Amnon killed and flees to Geshur.
events.detail: Tamar’s speech in verses 12–13 is clear and reasoned. She names the act as a disgrace in Israel. She names her own shame and his ruin. She even offers a lawful way through the king. Verse 14 says he would not listen. Her father is angry and silent (verse 21). Her brother tells her to keep quiet (verse 20).

events.title: The woman of Tekoa and Absalom’s return
events.summary: Joab sees that David longs for Absalom. He sends a wise woman from Tekoa to the king in mourning clothes. She says one of her sons killed the other in a fight. Her clan now demands the life of the son who is left. David promises to protect him. She then asks why the king does not bring back his own banished son. David guesses that Joab is behind it and lets Absalom return. For two years Absalom may not see the king’s face.
events.detail: The woman’s method copies Nathan’s in chapter 12. She wins a ruling on an invented case and then applies it. Verse 14 is her main argument. Death is final, like water spilled on the ground. God, she says, finds ways to bring the banished back. Her case differs from Absalom’s, who planned his killing for two years (13:23–28). David brings him back but will not see him (verse 24).

events.title: Absalom gathers support and David leaves Jerusalem
events.summary: Absalom gets a chariot, horses, and fifty runners. He stands by the gate and meets people who bring cases to the king. He tells each one that his claim is good and no one will hear it. So he steals the hearts of Israel. After four years he goes to Hebron and has himself declared king. David flees Jerusalem with his household and loyal foreign troops. He sends the ark back to the city with the priests. He climbs the Mount of Olives weeping and sends Hushai to act as a spy.
events.detail: Absalom never hears a case in this chapter. He tells every visitor the same thing: your claim is right (verse 3). In verse 4 he wishes aloud to be judge. He greets people as equals and will not let them bow (verse 5). The text does not say whether the courts were truly neglected. Verse 6 calls the result theft. David, by contrast, refuses to use the ark for his own cause (verses 25–26).

events.title: Ziba’s accusation, Shimei’s curses, and Absalom’s public act
events.summary: Ziba meets the fleeing king with donkeys, bread, fruit, and wine. He says Mephibosheth stayed in Jerusalem hoping to gain Saul’s kingdom. David gives Ziba all of Mephibosheth’s property. At Bahurim a man of Saul’s family named Shimei curses David and throws stones. Abishai wants to cut off his head. David says to leave him; perhaps the LORD told him to curse. Absalom enters Jerusalem, and Hushai pretends to serve him. On Ahithophel’s advice Absalom takes his father’s concubines in public.
events.detail: David decides a property case in verse 4 on one man’s word. The accused is absent and cannot answer. Ziba arrives with gifts, and he gains from the charge he brings. Mephibosheth’s side is heard only in 19:24–27. David lost support to a son who promised fair hearings (15:4). Here he gives an unfair one himself. With Shimei in verses 10–12 he is far more patient.

events.title: Hushai’s counsel and the messengers’ escape
events.summary: Ahithophel advises Absalom to strike David that night with twelve thousand men. Hushai argues for waiting and gathering all Israel. Absalom prefers Hushai’s advice, as the LORD intended. Hushai sends warning to David through the priests’ two sons. A boy sees them, and they hide in a well at Bahurim. A woman covers the well and sends the searchers away. David crosses the Jordan that night, and Ahithophel hangs himself. At Mahanaim three men bring beds, bowls, and food to David’s people.
events.detail: David’s survival depends on a chain of ordinary people. Hushai tells the priests, and a servant girl carries the word (verses 15–17). In verse 18 a householder’s well becomes the hiding place. His wife covers it and misleads the searchers (verses 19–20). Bahurim is also Shimei’s town (16:5), so one village holds both sides. Verse 14 gives the writer’s view of the cause. Machir, who brings supplies in verse 27, once sheltered Mephibosheth (9:4).

events.title: Absalom dies and David grieves
events.summary: David divides his army under Joab, Abishai, and Ittai. The men will not let him fight. He orders the three to deal gently with Absalom, and all the soldiers hear it. David’s men win in the forest of Ephraim. Absalom’s head catches in an oak, and his mule runs on. A soldier refuses to touch him, but Joab stabs him. Two runners carry the news to the king. David asks only about Absalom and weeps, “My son, my son!”
events.detail: Verse 5 notes that the whole army heard the king’s order. A soldier quotes it to Joab in verse 12 as his reason for holding back. Joab knows the order and breaks it (verse 14). He acts for the kingdom: a living Absalom is a living revolt. David asks both runners the same question (verses 29 and 32). His question is a father’s, not a king’s. Verse 33 gives his answer to the victory.

events.title: David returns and hears competing claims
events.summary: Joab tells David that his weeping shames the men who saved him. David sits in the gate, and the people come to him. He invites Judah to bring him back and promises Joab’s post to Amasa. Shimei begs forgiveness at the Jordan, and David spares him. Mephibosheth comes unwashed and says Ziba deceived him. David tells the two to divide the land. Old Barzillai declines a place at court and sends Chimham. Israel and Judah then quarrel over who has more claim to the king.
events.detail: Two men have told David opposite stories about the same land. Verse 24 supports Mephibosheth: he had not groomed himself since the king left. In verse 29 David cuts the question short. He splits the land and decides nothing about the truth. Mephibosheth answers that Ziba may take it all (verse 30). The pardon of Shimei is also not final (1 Kings 2:8–9). The quarrel in verses 41–43 leads straight into the next revolt.

events.title: Sheba’s revolt and the wise woman of Abel
events.summary: Sheba, a man of Benjamin, calls Israel to leave David, and the northern tribes follow. David sets apart the ten concubines Absalom took. Amasa is slow to gather Judah’s army. Joab greets Amasa as a brother and stabs him. Joab’s army besieges Sheba in the town of Abel. A wise woman calls to Joab from the wall. She persuades the town to throw Sheba’s head over to him. Joab withdraws, and a list of David’s officers follows.
events.detail: Joab is battering the wall when a woman asks to speak (verses 15–16). In verse 19 she names her town “a mother in Israel.” She calls it part of the LORD’s inheritance. Joab must then state what he really wants: one man (verse 21). She takes that to the people “in her wisdom” (verse 22). One death ends a siege that would have killed many. Abigail and the woman of Tekoa also stopped armed men with words.

events.title: Rizpah guards the dead and warriors defend David
events.summary: A famine lasts three years, and David asks the LORD why. The answer is that Saul killed Gibeonites, breaking Israel’s old oath. The Gibeonites ask for seven of Saul’s male descendants. David spares Mephibosheth and hands over seven others. They are hanged on a hill at the start of barley harvest. Rizpah, mother of two of them, guards the bodies until the rain comes. David hears of it and buries the bones with Saul’s and Jonathan’s. Four giants later fall to David’s men.
events.detail: Rizpah could not stop the executions. Verse 10 shows what she could do. She stays on the rock from harvest until rain, day and night. Deuteronomy 21:22–23 required burial the same day. Her watch is reported to the king (verse 11). Only then does David gather the bones and bury them properly (verses 12–14). Verse 14 places God’s answer for the land after that burial.

events.title: David’s song of deliverance
events.summary: David sings this song after the LORD rescues him from Saul and all his enemies. He calls the LORD his rock, fortress, and shield. Death’s waves surrounded him, and he cried out. The earth shook, and the LORD came down in storm and fire. He drew David out of deep waters. David says the LORD rewarded his clean hands. With God’s help he can run through a troop and leap a wall. The song ends with kindness to David and his descendants forever.
events.detail: The song is nearly the same as Psalm 18. Verse 36 credits David’s strength to gifts: a shield and God’s gentleness. He says that gentleness, not his own skill, made him great. The heading in verse 1 ties the song to his rescue from Saul. Verses 21–25 claim clean hands and kept ways. That fits the David of the cave, not of chapter 11. The book places the song here and leaves the contrast for the reader.

events.title: Last words and remembered warriors
events.summary: David’s last words say a ruler must be just and fear God. Such a ruler is like morning light after rain. God has made a lasting covenant with his house. The chapter then lists David’s mighty men and their deeds. One stood alone in a field and fought until his hand stuck to his sword. Three broke through Philistine lines to bring David water from Bethlehem’s well. Benaiah killed a lion in a pit on a snowy day. The list of the Thirty ends with Uriah the Hittite.
events.detail: David’s wish in verse 15 is spoken aloud, not given as an order. Three men risk their lives to grant it (verse 16). In verse 17 he will not drink. He calls the water the blood of the men who went. He pours it out to the LORD, as blood was poured out. The act honors their risk more than drinking would. The list ends in verse 39 with the name of a man David betrayed.

events.title: The census, plague, and Araunah’s threshing floor
events.summary: The LORD is angry with Israel, and David is moved to count the people. Joab objects, but the king insists. The count takes almost ten months. Then David’s heart troubles him, and he confesses. The prophet Gad offers three punishments, and David chooses to fall into the LORD’s hand. A plague kills seventy thousand. The angel stops at the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. David buys the floor, builds an altar, and the plague ends.
events.detail: Araunah offers the floor, the oxen, and the wood for free (verses 22–23). David’s refusal in verse 24 gives a rule for offerings. A gift to God that costs the giver nothing is no gift. The plague came through David’s own act (verse 10). A free altar would move the cost onto another man. In verse 17 David asks that the punishment fall on him and his house. Second Chronicles 3:1 places the later temple at this floor.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Strong evidence supports this route. The line shows a general path. Its branches and exact roadbeds changed over time.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The main connection is well supported. The line shows a broad route, not one fixed or fully built road.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The hill route is well supported. The exact track could divide or shift between nearby ridges and towns.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The valley route is well supported. The line combines several possible tracks. It does not mark specific river crossings.

ancientRoads.title: Shephelah road
ancientRoads.summary: This route ran through Judah’s western lowlands. It joined Beersheba, Lachish, Gezer, Aphek, and the valleys below Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.detail: The Shephelah formed a connected lowland zone between the coastal plain and the Judean hills. Fortified towns near the route guarded approaches into the highlands.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional route is well supported. Local branches between valleys and fortified towns are simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass and connection are well supported. The line does not claim an exact roadbed at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Lachish–Jerusalem approaches
ancientRoads.summary: Routes through the Shephelah valleys connected Lachish with Jerusalem. They also joined nearby walled towns with the Judean hills.
ancientRoads.detail: Second Kings 18:17 sends an Assyrian army from Lachish up to Jerusalem. The text does not name the road. This line shows one common approach.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is probable. The exact track is unknown, so the line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection is well supported. The displayed bends are approximate and do not identify one preserved Iron Age roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route crossed the Transjordan plateau. It passed Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Gilead before reaching Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: This broad route is well known. It was not one fully built road. Its path and local branches remain uncertain.

ancientRoads.title: Damascus–Hamath–Aleppo route
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south inland route connected Damascus with the Orontes valley, Hamath, and Aleppo.
ancientRoads.detail: Aleppo stood where many major routes met. They linked Anatolia, Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean. This line follows the broad route through the Orontes valley, not the desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is well supported. The evidence does not show one fixed Iron Age track. The line is dashed.

regions.name: Israel under David and Solomon · approximate
regions.summary: The Bible says Saul, David, and Solomon ruled all the tribes as one kingdom. Scholars disagree on how large it was.
regions.detail: David takes Jerusalem and makes it his capital (2 Samuel 5). Solomon builds the temple there, and the kingdom splits after his death.
regions.uncertainty: The shape covers the tribal lands from Dan to Beersheba. It leaves out lands that paid tribute.

regions.name: Philistine cities · approximate
regions.summary: Five Philistine cities held the southern coast: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, and Gath.
regions.detail: David defeats the Philistines after he becomes king (2 Samuel 5). Earlier he had lived among them at Gath and Ziklag.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Each city had its own ruler.

regions.name: Phoenician cities · approximate
regions.summary: Tyre, Sidon, and other coast cities each had their own king. They lived by ships and trade.
regions.detail: Hiram king of Tyre sends cedar and builders to David and Solomon. Solomon pays him in wheat and oil (1 Kings 5).
regions.uncertainty: The shape joins separate cities along one coast. They were never one kingdom.

regions.name: Aram of Damascus · approximate
regions.summary: Aram was a kingdom centered on Damascus. Assyria ended it in 732 BCE.
regions.detail: David defeats Aram of Damascus and puts garrisons there (2 Samuel 8:5–6). Rezon later rules Damascus against Solomon (1 Kings 11:23–25).
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Aram and Israel traded control of Gilead and Bashan.

regions.name: Ammon · approximate
regions.summary: Ammon was a kingdom east of the Jordan. Its chief city was Rabbah, now Amman.
regions.detail: Ammon shames David’s messengers, and war follows (2 Samuel 10). Joab takes Rabbah in 2 Samuel 12.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the land around Rabbah.

regions.name: Moab · approximate
regions.summary: Moab was a kingdom on the high land east of the Dead Sea. Dibon was its capital.
regions.detail: David defeats Moab and makes it pay tribute (2 Samuel 8:2).
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Numbers 21:26 says Moab once lost land north of the Arnon.

regions.name: Edom · approximate
regions.summary: Edom was a kingdom south of the Dead Sea. The Bible calls its people the children of Esau.
regions.detail: David puts garrisons in Edom (2 Samuel 8:14). Hadad of Edom later troubles Solomon (1 Kings 11).
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Edom’s people later moved west into southern Judah.

regions.name: Egypt · approximate
regions.summary: Egypt’s kings ruled the Nile valley and delta.
regions.detail: Solomon marries Pharaoh’s daughter (1 Kings 3:1). Jeroboam flees to Shishak king of Egypt (1 Kings 11:40).
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Egypt’s ruling families and power changed across these centuries.

guides.title: 2 Samuel: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: A promise raises the stakes of royal conduct
steps.text: The chapter turns on two meanings of “house.” David offers the LORD a building (verse 2). The LORD offers David a family of kings (verse 11). Verse 13 joins both: the son builds, and God secures his throne. Verses 14–15 add a limit and a guarantee. A sinning king will be punished, yet the kindness will not be removed. Even Nathan’s first answer is corrected the same night (verses 3–5).

steps.title: A story makes unequal power visible
steps.text: Nathan lets David judge the case before he knows it is his own. The poor man’s lamb was “like a daughter” to him (verse 3). David’s anger at the rich man is real (verses 5–6). Verse 7 turns his verdict back on him. The LORD’s speech lists what he gave David (verses 7–8). Verse 9 then says what David took. The penalties in verses 10–11 match the crimes: the sword and the wives.

steps.title: An offering must cost the giver something
steps.text: Araunah offers the floor, the oxen, and the wood for free (verses 22–23). David’s refusal in verse 24 gives a rule for offerings. A gift to God that costs the giver nothing is no gift. The plague came through David’s own act (verse 10). A free altar would move the cost onto another man. In verse 17 David asks that the punishment fall on him and his house. Second Chronicles 3:1 places the later temple at this floor.

chapterMaps.narrative: David is back in Ziklag when a man arrives from Saul’s camp. The man is an Amalekite, and he carries Saul’s crown and bracelet. He says the wounded Saul asked him for a final blow. David and his men tear their clothes and fast until evening. David has the man put to death for killing the LORD’s anointed. Then David sings a lament for Saul and Jonathan. Three times it cries, “How the mighty have fallen!” He orders the people of Judah to learn it.

Abner, Saul’s general, makes Saul’s son Ishbosheth king over the other tribes. The two armies meet at the pool of Gibeon. A contest of twelve against twelve turns into a battle. Joab’s brother Asahel chases Abner, ignores two warnings, and is killed. At sunset Abner calls for a halt, and Joab stops the pursuit.

Abner is furious and offers to bring all Israel to David. David first demands Michal back, and her husband follows her weeping. Abner meets David and leaves in peace. Joab calls him back and stabs him at the gate for Asahel’s death. David curses Joab’s house and leads the mourning for Abner. He says Zeruiah’s sons are too hard for him.

Two of Ishbosheth’s captains, Rechab and Baanah, enter his house at noon. They kill him on his bed and cut off his head. They carry it all night to David at Hebron. They say the LORD has avenged David on Saul’s family. David recalls the messenger he executed at Ziklag. He has the two men killed and buries the head in Abner’s tomb.

chapterMaps.narrative: David’s son Amnon desires his half sister Tamar. On a cousin’s advice he pretends to be ill and asks her to bring food. He seizes her, and she pleads with him. He rapes her, then hates her and has her thrown out. Tamar tears her royal robe and goes away crying. Her brother Absalom takes her into his house. David is very angry but does nothing. He tells each one that his claim is good and no one will hear it. So he steals the hearts of Israel. After four years he goes to Hebron and has himself declared king. David flees Jerusalem with his household and loyal foreign troops. He sends the ark back to the city with the priests. He climbs the Mount of Olives weeping and sends Hushai to act as a spy.

textRoutes.title: Two kingdoms and the battle at Gibeon
textRoutes.summary: David asks the LORD and moves to Hebron. The men of Judah anoint him king there. He thanks Jabesh Gilead for burying Saul. Abner, Saul’s general, makes Saul’s son Ishbosheth king over the other tribes. The two armies meet at the pool of Gibeon. A contest of twelve against twelve turns into a battle. Joab’s brother Asahel chases Abner, ignores two warnings, and is killed. At sunset Abner calls for a halt, and Joab stops the pursuit.
textRoutes.detail: Abner’s plea in verse 26 calls both armies “brothers.” He asks whether the sword must devour forever. Yet Abner proposed the deadly contest that began the day (verse 14). Joab accepts the halt and blows the trumpet (verse 28). The count is unequal: twenty dead against three hundred sixty (verses 30–31). Asahel’s death is not settled by the truce. Joab repays it in 3:27.

textRoutes.title: Abner changes allegiance and Joab kills him
textRoutes.summary: The war between Saul’s house and David’s house lasts a long time. Ishbosheth accuses Abner over one of Saul’s concubines. Abner is furious and offers to bring all Israel to David. David first demands Michal back, and her husband follows her weeping. Abner meets David and leaves in peace. Joab calls him back and stabs him at the gate for Asahel’s death. David curses Joab’s house and leads the mourning for Abner. He says Zeruiah’s sons are too hard for him.
textRoutes.detail: Abner’s death helps David, and people could suspect him. Verse 28 is his public denial before the LORD. He adds a curse on Joab’s house in verse 29. He walks behind the body, weeps, and fasts (verses 31–35). Verse 37 says all the people understood it was not his doing. Still he does not punish Joab. In verse 39 he admits he is too weak to control him.

textRoutes.title: David becomes king of Israel and takes Jerusalem
textRoutes.summary: All the tribes come to Hebron and anoint David king over Israel. He is thirty years old and reigns forty years in all. He captures the stronghold of Zion from the Jebusites. Jerusalem becomes the City of David. Hiram king of Tyre sends cedar and craftsmen to build him a house. David takes more wives and has more children. The Philistines attack twice in the Valley of Rephaim. Each time David asks the LORD and wins.
textRoutes.detail: Verse 12 gives the purpose of David’s success. The LORD raised his kingdom “for his people Israel’s sake.” The palace and the throne are means to that end. The next verse reports more wives and concubines (verse 13). Deuteronomy 17:17 warned kings against exactly that. The text sets the two verses together without comment. In verses 19 and 23 David asks before each battle and gets different orders.

textRoutes.title: The ark reaches Jerusalem
textRoutes.summary: David gathers thirty thousand men to bring the ark to Jerusalem. They carry it on a new cart, and Uzzah touches it and dies. David is angry and afraid and leaves it at Obed-Edom’s house. The LORD blesses that house for three months. David then brings the ark up with sacrifices, dancing in a linen ephod. Saul’s daughter Michal watches from a window and despises him. He blesses the people and gives everyone food. Michal mocks his display, and she has no child to her death.
textRoutes.detail: The chapter calls Michal “the daughter of Saul” three times (verses 16, 20, 23). It does not call her David’s wife here. In verse 20 she speaks for a king’s dignity before servants. David answers that the LORD chose him above her father (verse 21). Their history is long and painful. She loved him and saved him, then was given away and taken back. Verse 23 means no child will join the two royal houses.

textRoutes.title: Amnon assaults Tamar and Absalom takes revenge
textRoutes.summary: David’s son Amnon desires his half sister Tamar. On a cousin’s advice he pretends to be ill and asks her to bring food. He seizes her, and she pleads with him. He rapes her, then hates her and has her thrown out. Tamar tears her royal robe and goes away crying. Her brother Absalom takes her into his house. David is very angry but does nothing. Two years later Absalom has Amnon killed and flees to Geshur.
textRoutes.detail: Tamar’s speech in verses 12–13 is clear and reasoned. She names the act as a disgrace in Israel. She names her own shame and his ruin. She even offers a lawful way through the king. Verse 14 says he would not listen. Her father is angry and silent (verse 21). Her brother tells her to keep quiet (verse 20).

textRoutes.title: Absalom gathers support and David leaves Jerusalem
textRoutes.summary: Absalom gets a chariot, horses, and fifty runners. He stands by the gate and meets people who bring cases to the king. He tells each one that his claim is good and no one will hear it. So he steals the hearts of Israel. After four years he goes to Hebron and has himself declared king. David flees Jerusalem with his household and loyal foreign troops. He sends the ark back to the city with the priests. He climbs the Mount of Olives weeping and sends Hushai to act as a spy.
textRoutes.detail: Absalom never hears a case in this chapter. He tells every visitor the same thing: your claim is right (verse 3). In verse 4 he wishes aloud to be judge. He greets people as equals and will not let them bow (verse 5). The text does not say whether the courts were truly neglected. Verse 6 calls the result theft. David, by contrast, refuses to use the ark for his own cause (verses 25–26).
